articles.title: Will Smith is in a slump, but benching him isn't an option for Dodgers
articles.summary: Will Smith's vital contributions at catcher mean the Dodgers can't afford to bench him even though he has struggled mightily at the plate this postseason.
articles.body:
The Dodgers have a big hole in the middle of their batting order, and it's not Shohei Ohtani .

If anything, Ohtani has reemerged as an offensive force in the cleanup spot, singling, walking and scoring the Dodgers' only run Sunday in a 2-1 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 1 of the National League Championship Series .

The problem is with the guy hitting in front of Ohtani.

Will Smith walked in four plate appearances, marking just the second time he's reached base in the postseason. In the four division series games against the Atlanta Braves, he had a single in 16 at-bats, striking out seven times. He's hitting .053 in the playoffs — only Cleveland's Ángel Martínez has a lower average among players with at least nine at-bats.

But there's not much the Dodgers can do about it. They are built to win with pitching and Smith, the catcher, is the guy they rely on to guide those pitchers through games.

Dalton Rushing , who started just three fewer games behind the plate than Smith this season, is injured and not on the roster. Hunter Feduccia , who did make the team, caught just 15 complete games this season and isn't an option to start in the playoffs.

"I'm not going to put Feduccia in place of Will Smith," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. "That's just not going to happen."

So Roberts and the Dodgers are left to muddle on with Smith regardless of how much he struggles offensively. That's because he's far more valuable crouching behind the plate than standing next to it.

"I don't even know how he's performing offensively," said Tarik Skubal , who took the loss Sunday. "Catchers, I think it's the most important position on the field. They're the ones calling pitches, dictating game flow, rhythm, all that type of stuff. I'm going to trust those guys always."

Smith appears to be executing his catching duties very well, since opponents have scored just 10 runs and are hitting .160 against the Dodgers this postseason. Only Tampa Bay, which has played two fewer games, has done better.

As for what Smith thinks, that's unknown because the Dodgers did not make him available to the media Sunday. But since he's not coming out of the lineup, the next-best solution might be moving him to another spot in the order.

That worked with Ohtani, who had as many strikeouts as hits in the first two games of the division series, when he batted second. Since being dropped in the order, he has reached base four times in three games, stolen a base and scored twice.

"There's always lineup construction. I can think it through. He's not swinging the bat well," Roberts said of Smith. "It's hard because of the body of work, he just has that knack to get a hit, to get a big hit."

That's exactly what happened last fall when Smith's two-out, 11th-inning home run in Game 7 of the World Series helped the Dodgers win a second straight title .

Smith was on the injured list for 86 days this summer because of neck disk inflammation, returning for the final month when he slashed .290/.400/.548. He has cooled off considerably in October, just as he did last year, when he returned from a right hand contusion three games into the playoffs and got just two hits in his first 14 at-bats.

He recovered to bat .400 in last year's NLCS win over Milwaukee, then broke a 4-4 tie with his winning homer against the Toronto Blue Jays. Just as important, though, Smith caught all but 11 innings in the Dodgers' final 15 postseason games — including two 11-inning games and another that lasted 18 innings.

Smith rarely has hit well in the postseason, batting just .206 in 18 series, which may explain Roberts' lack of panic. Plus, Roberts knows his All-Star catcher has helped him win three World Series rings, and if the Dodgers are to get another, it will be on the strength of their pitching, not their hitting.

And that side of Smith's game is as strong as ever.

"To be honest, that's not where my focus is with Will," Skubal said of his catcher's hitting. "My focus is what he's doing behind the dish and he's very important. He's very important to the entire pitching staff."

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Dodgers drop Game 1 of NLCS in Milwaukee
articles.summary: The Dodgers had their chances. They had runners in scoring position, chased Jacob Misiorowski from the mound before he could complete five innings, and recei...
articles.body:
MILWAUKEE — The Dodgers had their chances. They had runners in scoring position, chased Jacob Misiorowski from the mound before he could complete five innings, and received three scoreless innings from their bullpen. But when the Dodgers needed one final swing to change the outcome, Mookie Betts came up short.

The Dodgers dropped Game 1 of the National League Championship Series on Sunday, falling 2-1 to the Milwaukee Brewers at American Family Field. The Dodgers now trail 0-1 in the series, and Milwaukee has already accomplished something it couldn't do last postseason: take the opening game and put itself in position to avoid another sweep at the hands of the Dodgers.

With Game 1 decided by a single run, the Dodgers were left to wonder what might have been after repeatedly failing to capitalize on their scoring opportunities.

The final chance came in the ninth inning.

After pinch hitter Josue De Paula worked a walk to put runners on first and second, the Dodgers brought the potential tying run into scoring position. Betts, who led off for the Dodgers with Shohei Ohtani batting fourth, stepped to the plate with an opportunity to extend the game.

Instead, Betts lifted a deep fly ball to center field, ending the game and sending Milwaukee into celebration.

For a Dodgers team accustomed to playing deep into October, the loss was a frustrating start to a series that figures to test both clubs.

"It's going to be a long series. We knew it coming in," Dave Roberts said.

Roberts reiterated that sentiment when discussing Milwaukee's position as the team with the best regular-season record in baseball.

"You can't go into a long series against a team that has the best record in baseball and expect to just win 4. It's going to be a long series, we knew it coming in," Roberts said.

The Dodgers' offense never found the consistent rhythm needed to overcome Milwaukee's pitching.

The Dodgers managed five hits against Misiorowski, who worked 4⅓ innings and allowed one run while striking out five and walking three. The Dodgers eventually forced the Brewers to turn to their bullpen, but the damage never materialized into a comeback.

Andy Pages accounted for the Dodgers' lone run with a second-inning RBI single. Beyond that, the Dodgers struggled to turn baserunners into runs, leaving several opportunities unfinished.

One of the most significant moments came in the sixth inning, when the Dodgers had runners on the corners against Abner Uribe. With a chance to tie the game or take the lead, Pages struck out to end the threat.

That failure loomed large as Milwaukee's bullpen continued to shut down the Dodgers.

The ninth inning offered one final opportunity, but Betts' flyout ensured the Dodgers would leave Milwaukee without a win to open the series.

Skubal Keeps Dodgers in the Fight, but Brewers Take Control

The pitching matchup between Tarik Skubal and Misiorowski delivered the kind of tense October baseball expected from two teams with championship aspirations.

Skubal struck out seven over five innings, allowing five hits, two walks and two earned runs on 81 pitches. Although he escaped a bases-loaded jam in the fifth, Milwaukee eventually found the breakthrough it needed.

Garrett Mitchell opened the inning with a walk before Cooper Pratt moved him into scoring position with a bunt. Luis Lara followed with an RBI single, bringing Mitchell home to give the Brewers a 2-1 advantage.

Roberts turned to Alex Vesia for the left-handed portion of Milwaukee's lineup after Skubal completed his outing. The Dodgers' bullpen delivered three scoreless innings, keeping the deficit at one run and giving the offense an opportunity to respond.

It was a strong relief effort, but the Dodgers couldn't provide the tying run.

Despite the disappointment, the Dodgers were quick to emphasize that one loss does not define a seven-game series.

Freddie Freeman acknowledged the frustration while keeping the team's focus on the bigger picture.

"Any loss in the playoffs is not great, but it's a long series. It's just the first game," Freeman said.

Freeman also expressed confidence heading into Monday, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto scheduled to take the ball for Game 2.

"It's just the first game. We'll come back out tomorrow with Yamamoto, I feel pretty confident," Freeman said.

Betts delivered a similar message following his game-ending flyout.

"We got to focus on the task at hand, and that's winning the game tomorrow," Betts said.

For a Dodgers club that entered the postseason with championship expectations, the challenge now is to turn that confidence into a response on the field.

One of the Dodgers' other concerns entering Game 2 is the production of Will Smith.

Smith went 0-for-3 in the opener and has yet to look like his usual self since returning from the injured list. His continued struggles have raised questions about whether the Dodgers might consider giving Hunter Feduccia an opportunity behind the plate.

Roberts, however, made his position clear.

"I'm not going to put Feduccia in place of Will Smith," Roberts said.

The Dodgers are sticking with their veteran catcher, trusting that his experience and offensive ability will eventually translate into better results.

With the series just beginning, Roberts appears unwilling to make a drastic lineup change based on one game.

Yamamoto Gets the Ball With the Series on the Line

The Dodgers won't have much time to dwell on Sunday's defeat. Game 2 arrives Monday afternoon, with Yamamoto tasked with helping the Dodgers avoid falling into an 0-2 hole before the series shifts back to Los Angeles.

Roberts made it clear that he remains confident in his starter.

"They got Henderson, we got Yamamoto. We feel good with our guy," Roberts said.

He reinforced that belief when discussing the urgency of the next game.

"We've got our guy going tomorrow, who we trust undoubtedly. We need to win a baseball game."

The message was straightforward: the Dodgers don't need to solve the entire series on Monday. They need to even it.

Milwaukee, meanwhile, has already secured the result it wanted. After being swept by the Dodgers in last year's postseason meeting, the Brewers have struck first and put the pressure on the defending champions.

The Dodgers still have plenty of baseball ahead of them, but Sunday's loss exposed the importance of converting scoring opportunities when the margins are this thin.

A second-inning RBI single from Pages wasn't enough. Three scoreless innings from the bullpen weren't enough. And a late rally that put the tying run within reach ultimately ended with Betts' fly ball to end of the game.

Yamamoto takes the mound Monday, and the Dodgers will look to leave American Family Field with the series tied before heading back to Dodger Stadium for Game 3 on Wednesday.

As Roberts made clear after Game 1, this series was never expected to be easy.

The Dodgers have their first setback. Their response will determine how much it matters.

articles.title: Riftbound: Radiance Hands-On Preview and Interview - Riftbound Embraces Complexity
articles.summary: I played Riftbound fifth set, Radiance, in Pre-Rift and sealed formats and spoke with executive producer Chengran Chai, who spoke on how Deploy is primed to disrupt the meta and more.
articles.body:
Riftbound’s final set of the year, Radiance , is finally upon us, and I went hands-on with the cards at a very early Pre-Rift tournament. This marks the League of Legends TCG’s fifth set, and features musically-inspired designs and brand new mechanics poised to disrupt the meta.

I also had the chance to talk with Chengran Chai, the executive producer of Riftbound, to get some insight about the set straight from the source in a joint interview with Temple of Geek’s Myles Obenza.

First, a quick recap of the new mechanics being introduced in Radiance, with some of Chai’s commentary:

New Radiance Keywords: Disarm, Show Off, Deploy

Disarm is the simplest of the new mechanics: When your unit with Disarm attacks , it reduces the might of an enemy unit at that battlefield, usually by one. It immediately made me think of Ahri’s original abilities, which is fitting, since the new green (Calm) Ahri, Confident, comes with Disarm. Her unit has a built-in buff when you reduce the Might of an enemy unit, gaining +1 Might herself. The promising new blue (Mind) Kai’sa, Rebel, has both Disarm and gives spells Reaction speed when in a showdown.

Show Off is a mechanic that might be familiar to you if you’ve played other popular TCGs. Cards with Show Off gain an additional effect if you “Show Off” a qualifying card to your opponent as you play it. We’ve only seen four cards in Radiance with Show Off so far–two units and two spells–and they each grant totally different effects. The 5-cost yellow (Order) Spell Rousing Display (clearly part of the Legend Seraphine’s kit) plays four 1-Might Recruit Tokens to your base instead of just one if you Show Off a card with Energy cost 7 or more.

Chai said that Show Off is a trade off–you’re giving away information in exchange for something, but TCGs are very much a game of information. “If I’m planning a spell heavy deck, whether you have Defy or not in your hand matters a great deal to me,” Chai explained. “Show Off basically opens up another dimension to the kind of like, 3D, 4D chess–that’s 5D.” Maybe you show your opponent something you have on purpose to throw them off, pushing them into a play you have the perfect counter-play for. Show Off has the possibility of granting great effects, but it opens the game up for more mind games, too.

Deploy is a keyword specifically for Gear, allowing you to deploy that Gear straight to a Battlefield. While there, it’ll provide an effect, but will be killed if your opponent holds the Battlefield it’s at.

“I think Deploy is probably the one that will disrupt [the meta], because historically, you don't think of just going straight to a battlefield,” Chai said. “And now you have, like, Jarvan IV’s E-Q, you have Ziggs just tossing bombs onto battlefields, and it's going to change the way people think about Defending quite a bit.” Jarvan IV’s “E-Q” that Chai references is the move combo in League of Legends where he throws his flag and then pulls himself there–pretty 1-to-1 with Jarvan IV’s Legend ability in Riftbound, which lets you move a friendly unit to a Battlefield when you play a Gear with Deploy there (and pay 1 Power).

Orianna's Legend ability allows you to turn a friendly Gear into a Gear Unit at the start of your Main Phase, a pretty tricky and cool thing you can do to steal some points with Deployable Gear! Her Signature Gear, The Ball, is especially interesting as it also gains Ganking, allowing it to roll back and forth between battlefields each turn. Chai seemed to be especially high on Orianna along with Deploy, noting her Legend and The Ball as playable cards he'd want to showcase from this set.

Both Show Off and Deploy up the complexity of Riftbound. But, Deploy and Disarm seem to be mechanics that will absolutely disrupt defensive Hold strategies the most, which is especially scary for me as someone who’s playing Akali and Vex with Astral Heron hold strategies!

Last time I got to play with a set early, it was strictly with a preconstructed showcase deck behind closed doors, and I didn’t have more than thirty minutes to actually play with the cards. This time, however, we got a Pre-Rift tournament plus packs to take home to tinker with. So, I played Radiance with one seeded Pre-Rift deck and built two “Sealed” decks to test out–some of which were more successful than others!

In my Radiance Pre-Rift Kit, I got the orange (Body) and yellow (Order) Jarvan IV, Exemplar of Demacia Legend. Jarvan’s Legend ability makes use of the new Deploy keyword: “When you play a gear with [Deploy], you may exhaust me and pay [1 Power] to move a friendly unit to that battlefield.”

I threw in plenty of Gears with Deploy, cards with Gear synergies, plus a couple purple (Chaos) cards that made Bombs, drew cards, and generated Gold so I’d have a decent supply of Power to activate Jarvan IV’s Legend Ability. I removed the 7-cost Jarvan IV, Royal Heir as my chosen Champion Unit, though, and replaced it with the K’Sante, Courageous I pulled. High-cost chosen champions aren’t generally the best move, especially in the speedy Pre-Rift format, and though K’sante still costs a pretty hefty 5 runes, having a Unit with Accelerate at my fingertips in the late game proved to be invaluable.

I can’t say I was thrilled at opening Jarvan IV at first (I was hoping for Riven or Evelynn), but after playing just a few turns, the deck strategy clicked spectacularly for me. I was also lucky enough to get a new battlefield called Hunter’s Circle, which reads, “For each player, the first unit or gear they play here on their turn costs 1 less,” which goes super well with Deployable Gear, since you can play them to the battlefield whenever you want on your turn!

In my first game, a test match, I went second. I played Concert Poster to Hunter’s Circle for free, allowing me to then play Skystrike Squadron for a reduced cost of 3 for returning Concert Poster to my hand. A 4-Might Unit with Reflect on my first turn: Not bad! On my next turn, I was able to create two Recruits with Concert Poster and Buff a Recruit and my Skystrike Squadron with Pillaged Armory. Maybe some godlike luck allowed for this to happen, but it felt pretty dang nifty!

With this build, I have to shoutout Portable Portal, a 2-cost orange (Body) Gear with Deploy. When I showed this card to someone, they said they knew it’d be a menace just because Teemo is on it. When you play it, you can pay one orange (Body) power to ready a Unit. Friendly units at that battlefield with Portable Portal also have Ganking. These abilities paired with the Jarvan IV Legend allowed for double conquering in one turn, or allowing for a Gank and then a retreat with Jarvan’s ability, protecting my Unit. It’s a rare card, though, so pulling it in a Pre-Rift isn’t exactly guaranteed!

In my two Sealed games, one of the decks had no discernible theme besides trying to make Seraphine work (I did not). In the other, I tried for a Ziggs / Bomb build because I happened to pull his Legend and his Epic-rarity red (Fury) Unit, Ziggs, Short-Fused. Let me tell you, the Bomb strategy is pretty tricky to hold together if you don’t have a very reliable way to detonate them on your opponent’s turn. Usually, they explode, dealing two damage per bomb when your opponent holds the battlefield they’re deployed at.

I found it fairly difficult to get enough bombs on a battlefield to matter in one turn unless I held with Explosimian, which lets you play three Bomb gear tokens to a single battlefield. Of course, this still does nothing for protecting you if you’re trying to hold your bomb-ridden battlefield. However, the Pre-Rift Seeded decks with the Ziggs Legend includes the 4-might purple (Chaos) Champion Unit Ziggs, Explosive, which allows you to kill a friendly gear when he defends! If you have enough Bombs, you could potentially wipe your opponent before they can even touch you. And if they can, well, Ziggs, Explosive gets +2 Might if he killed a friendly gear that turn!

Unfortunately, I did not have this Ziggs Unit in my Sealed game, so a different strategy was in order. We determined it’s likely best to load Bombs up one battlefield, leave them alone, and then build a strong Hold at the other Battlefield, forcing your opponent to choose to deal with either a battlefield fortified with Units or fortified with Bombs.

The Unit Reckless Innovator and Gear The Good Stuff, both The purple (Chaos) cards, also proved to be very useful in just about every thrown together deck I or my opponent played. I have a lot more opinions, but it’d be absurd to expect you to read my ramblings, so we’ll end it at that.

Overall, the Sealed and Pre-Rift formats for Radiance were very fun, and the new ideas this set brings to Riftbound add an even higher level of complexity to the existing pool. As for Radiance in a vacuum for Sealed, it seemed to allow for a good variety of unique deck-building options. This is of course by design.

“We want the base set to have a rich enough playing set,” Chai said. “Such that Sealed events are fun… all by itself.”

Riftbound: Radiance - Music ONs, SPs, and Alt Runes

With the playing set determined, that’s when the Riftbound team layers collectibility on top of it with Alt Art, Overnumbered, and SP cards. Some of the rare standouts for Radiance are Riot Games Music crossovers, including the Overnumbered Heartsteel cards, SP K/DA cards, and Overnumbered Ekko, Revolutionary, which features Ekko’s original True Damage skin. The Overnumbered cards also come in the Signature variety, which are the rarest pulls besides the single Ultimate Rare in this set.

“We knew Riot as a whole would have a music moment towards the end of the year, so very early on, we said we would lean into that,” Chai said. However, as a physical game, the Riftbound team needed to finalize many card details before the songs were even composed and the new character designs were finished. “That is why you see… for the K/DA and Heartsteel cards, it is very much their K/DA All Out and Heartsteel 1.0 versions, because the 2.0 versions just weren’t quite ready,” Chai said. “But we thought it would be a great way to showcase Riftbound’s participation… and leverage the broader music moment to allow more fans to see and experience Riftbound as well.”

This original plan didn’t even include teasing Heartsteel’s Riftbound cards in Heartsteel’s new Live My Life music video–the Riot Music Team actually initiated that easter egg, asking the Riftbound team if they wanted the cards in the music video. Of course, they said yes.

Though Riftbound has been very supported from within Riot since the beginning, the somewhat unexpected explosion of its popularity has given Riftbound even more opportunities to be a part of Riot-wide moments. Another example of this is the Riftbound easter egg in Valorant’s Aeris Flex cosmetic.

The Heartsteel Overnumbered cards feature a very unique design, akin to K-pop photo cards, complete with bright motifs, stickers, and Y2K elements. Playing into the photo card inspiration even more, the Heartsteel Overnumbered Signature cards are "signed" by the characters themselves--not the artists like on other Signature cards! Riot Games’ senior Manager of creative development Michelle Mauk spoke about the design process during the Radiance panel at the Riftbound Regional Qualifier (RQ) in Los Angeles , which I highly recommend you watch if you’re interested.

I always feel like renders of Overnumbered cards don’t do them justice, and that’s certainly the case for the Heartsteel cards, too. The texturing and foiling on Riftbound’s most coveted cards are always so impressive to behold in person.

Radiance’s Ultimate Rare ties well into the heavy music theme but is, shockingly, a Battlefield: Packed Amphitheater. This card will be the rarest card in all of Riftbound’s main sets, only appearing in about 0.025% of booster packs. That’s a huge rarity uptick from the only other Ultimate Rare, Baron Nasher from Unleashed, with a 0.1% pack rate. The in-person foiling and texturing you can't see in a render does a lot a lot of heavy lifting for this one–and you can get a better look at it, and see some creators’ reactions, in this official PlayRiftbound reel.

There are other Overnumbers and Alt Art cards to chase that aren’t musically inclined, too, like the Overnumbererd Mordekaiser Legend IGN exclusively revealed last week .

Radiance Pre-Rifts start at local game stores near you on Oct. 16, and I really can’t wait to play some more. With the complexity Radiance introduces, this might not be the best first set to get into, but it’s great for existing players craving more variety and creativity in their deck building. That being said, the Riftbound community has always been nothing but welcoming and helpful at every store I’ve played at, too, so don’t be shy. Otherwise, Radiance booster boxes, packs, and vaults will be available to purchase on Oct. 23.

Casey DeFreitas is the deputy editor of guides at IGN and is playing three more Riftbound Radiance Pre-Rifts this weekend at a local game store, because they're just that much fun. Catch her on socials @ShinyCaseyD .

articles.title: Latest Leaked GTA 6 Video Shows Lucia Fully Naked, Sparks Fan Skepticism
articles.summary: The GTA 6 leaker has reportedly released yet another unauthorized gameplay video, this time allegedly showing Lucia fully naked in a bid to push their crypto scheme. However, some now suspect Cyberleek is using a developer build or cheats to make Jason and Lucia naked, and that the leaked gameplay does not accurately represent GTA 6 as it will play at launch.
articles.body:
UPDATE: Cyberleek has reportedly followed through on their threat to release a “Lucia closeup 4k” video, and is once again tying further leaks to crypto market cap targets, ranging from $5 million to $25 million. According to online reports, Cyberleek has threatened to release a new unauthroized GTA 6 gameplay video every day, assuming the memecoin market cap targets are met. However, the Cyberleek memecoin has crashed, with a current market cap of $2.5 million.

Fans have spent the last week calling on people not to spend money on Cyberleek, pointing to the person or group's previous form when it came to cashing out in August. With GTA 6 little over a month away, it seems Cyberleek is doubling down on their crypto scheme one last time.

ORIGINAL STORY: The GTA 6 leaker has reportedly released yet another unauthorized gameplay video, this time allegedly showing Lucia fully naked in a bid to push their crypto scheme. However, some now suspect Cyberleek is using a developer build or cheats to make Jason and Lucia naked, and that the leaked gameplay does not accurately represent GTA 6 as it will play at launch.

Cyberleek had threatened to release gameplay showing Lucia fully naked if the market cap of their memecoin hit $4 million. That was achieved over the weekend. However, while the new video reportedly does show Lucia fully naked, there are a number of signs that some believe suggest Cyberleek has tinkered with the build they allegedly have access to .

One suspected telltale sign from the previous leak was that a tank was spawned into the game world, suggesting access to a dev menu of some kind. Now, with two leaked videos allegedly showing both Jason and Lucia fully naked but NPCs in the game world failing to react to that in any way, some believe this effect was achieved with either a dev menu or cheats.

In Pictures: How GTA 6's Jason and Lucia Have Evolved Since 2023

One theory is that Cyberleak was able to access this state for both Lucia and Jason because in at least one mission players will see both characters naked, perhaps in a nudist resort. As it stands, this is all speculation, and it is unknown if GTA 6 will feature either character naked at any point — officially at least.

Cyberleek has doubled down on their crypto scheme in the last week, threatening Rockstar and parent company Take-Two with the release of a full playthrough of the game’s story if they fail to release GTA 6 on-disc and issue a public apology — and the market cap of their memecoin hits $30 million. Of course, few believe these GTA 6 leaks are about campaigning for physical media — rather they're about making money from cryptocurrency.

To that end, Cyberleek has polled people on the release of a “Lucia closeup 4k video,” which suggests further leaks are incoming.

A cryptocurrency market capitalization (market cap) is the total dollar value of all the coins or tokens of a digital asset currently in circulation. At the time of this article’s publication, Cyberleek had a market cap of $2.7 million, having spiked at $8.4 million on October 11 as people pushed for the release of the latest gameplay. It seems unlikely that it will get anywhere near $30 million.

Cyberleek appeared to go dark after a spate of high-profile GTA 6 leaks in August that sparked an investigation from Rockstar parent company Take-Two. The company issued subpoenas to the likes of Discord as part of the hunt for the person or group of people responsible. But Cyberleek reemerged last week with the release of a 24-minute GTA 6 gameplay video that showed cutscenes, story beats, playable characters Jason and Lucia naked (in the case of Jason, full-frontal nudity), and a first-person camera.

It remains unclear how the gameplay footage, or any potential build of the game it's taken from, escaped the confines of Rockstar's infamous tight security. This week’s developments suggest Cyberleek remains at large and defiant in the face of potential legal action.

In August, Rockstar addressed the GTA 6 leaks , describing the situation as "heartbreaking" for its development team and "unfortunate" for fans. At the time, the developer acknowledged that its intended experience for players "may now be impacted by some spoilers," but reiterated GTA 6's previously-confirmed launch date of November 19.

Analysis of cryptocurrency transactions in late August pointed to the GTA 6 leaker having "cashed out," earning around $270,000 in the process. Every video posted by Cyberleek pointed to a website where fans could pay to vote on further leaks using the leaker's own cryptocurrency. Such a poll is reportedly live on Cyberleek's website now , suggesting yet another leak is on the way.

Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: Gears of War: E-Day Dev Confirms DDoS Attack
articles.summary: Gears of War: E-Day suffered a DDoS attack over the weekend, developer The Coalition has said.
articles.body:
Gears of War: E-Day suffered a DDoS attack over the weekend, developer The Coalition has said.

Players suffered intermittent disconnects and login issues while trying to play the Xbox Series X and S and PC action game, which The Coalition eventually got on top of. It has now confirmed the problems were the result of a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack targeting online services.

“Our teams are continuing to monitor and mitigate this activity. We’ll provide updates if there are any significant changes,” The Coalition said . “Thank you for your patience and understanding.”

There is a great deal of speculation online about the motivation behind hitting Gears with a DDoS attack, with some pointing to a continued online vendetta against the game for apparently being “woke.” E-Day has a “mostly positive” user review rating on Steam. Whatever the reason (there may be no overarching reason behind the DDoS attack at all), E-Day is now up and running.

Last week, Alinea Analytics' head of marketing analysis, Rhys Elliott, reported that E-Day had sold an estimated 230,000 copies in its first week in what was described as a soft start. These unofficial figures, which are not backed by data provided by Microsoft, pointed to Xbox subscription service Game Pass as cannibalizing sales.

Earlier this month, the boss of The Coalition responded to reports that staff at the studio were worried they might lose their jobs amid the ongoing cuts at Xbox, promising the next Gears game wouldn’t take as long to make.

Eurogamer had reported on internal concern that layoffs would hit The Coalition after the release of E-Day. "The mood is certainly 'let's not celebrate the game until we're three months post launch, just in case,' which is very unusual," one source told the site. "We're just expecting the next wave [of layoffs], or being reorganized under Activision or something later this year," claimed another.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma’s “reset” of Microsoft’s gaming business has seen nearly 2,000 people cut already this financial year, with more to come. A number of studios have left the business or are in the process of closing down. Microsoft has also reorganized its studios, bringing Halo and Sea of Thieves developer Rare under Call of Duty developer Activision, and Grounded developer Obsidian under Fallout developer Bethesda.

Of course, Gears of War: E-Day was selected to be an Xbox Series X and S and PC game, ditching any release for a sales-boosting PS5 version. The Coalition studio head Mike Crump recently told the BBC that success for E-Day goes behind sales, saying: "We measure things like, are we showcasing the platform? Are we pushing the hardware to its limits? Are we showcasing what the Xbox is capable of? ...Our goal basically is to be the best-looking game on the Xbox and really show the industry what's possible with our hardware.”

Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: Este juego de mesa de LEGO tiene algo que nunca había visto: ninjas que se transforman en cada partida
articles.standfirst: He estado jugando a LEGO Ninjago: Destiny's Bounty Adventures y tiene ideas muy interesantes.
articles.summary: He estado jugando a LEGO Ninjago: Destiny's Bounty Adventures y tiene ideas muy interesantes.
articles.body: Nunca antes había probado un juego de mesa basado en el universo LEGO, pero ahora me arrepiento de no haberlo hecho, y es que nunca había probado nada parecido. No sé si es el único que se hace así, pero que LEGO Ninjago: Destiny's Bounty Adventures transforme tus personajes a medida que avanza la partida es algo que me ha llamado mucho la atención. El juego se basa en la película, tal y como habréis podido inferir, y es un juego de aventura cooperativo en el que cada jugador manejará a un personaje: Kai, Nya, Cole o Zane. El montaje, en este caso, es muy sencillo. Aunque mantiene la esencia LEGO de conectar piezas, la preparación inicial es muy básica, por lo que no te llevará mucho tiempo preparar a los cuatro personajes antes de ponerte a jugar. Así pues, el interés no está únicamente en su apartado artístico (puro LEGO), sino en la capacidad que sus personajes nos ofrecen al cambiar de equipamiento según las cartas que usemos. Así pues, Ninjago: Destiny's Bounty Adventures propone una aventura cooperativa de dos a cuatro jugadores en la que habrá que defender el Botín del Destino de una invasión de villanos. El juego parece estar diseñado especialmente para los más peques de la casa, mas lo cierto es que lo estuve jugando con mis primos pequeños y también me lo pasé bien. Sea como fuere, ellos fueron los grandes protagonistas, siendo los que más disfrutaron de la experiencia al poder diseñar sus propios personajes. Es más, les vi cambiando piezas de sus diferentes ninjas para crear sus propios modelos de distintos colores. Es, sin duda, una de las grandes bazas de un juego de LEGO. Aunque tienes unas directrices originales, al final depende de ti mismo y de los jugadores escoger la dirección visual de cada personaje. Dicho esto, la idea es la misma sea cual sea la ruta: aprovechar las habilidades de cada ninja (cada uno tiene que elegir a un personaje, pues tienen sus propias piezas y características) mientras se trabaja en equipo para superar cualquier dificultad. La caja trae 124 elementos LEGO, cuatro minifiguras y varios mazos de cartas. Son estas las que nos permiten mejorar y alterar a los personajes a medida que el juego progresa. ¿Cómo? Mediante unas cartas de Potencial que nos permiten desbloquear mejoras para cada personaje. Así es. Estas mejoras tienen una representación física y visual a través de distintas piezas, por lo que los ninjas van obteniendo equipamiento tanto en el reglamento como de manera física. Cierto es que no se trata de una transformación completa, pero su evolución física a través de nuevas piezas de equipamiento ofrece variantes visuales muy tangibles que le dan mucha vida al juego. Es una de las cosas que más me llamó a mí la atención y de las que más les gustaron a mis primos pequeños. Por supuesto, todo tiene repercusión en el propio juego. Aunque esa evolución estética es lo que más llama la atención de buenas a primeras, no debemos olvidarnos de que es un juego de mesa defensivo. Tenemos que evitar que los villanos invadan nuestro barco a través de un juego en el que hay que gestionar movimientos sobre el tablero, usar habilidades y combinar ataques para derrotar a nuestros enemigos más poderosos. Es un juego en el que la cooperación es clave, teniendo que decidir cuándo es mejor afrontar un desafío de manera solitaria mientras los demás defienden otras zonas o cuándo es mejor juntarse para acabar pronto con un reto y seguir con la defensa. Lo bueno es que es un título bastante rejugable, pues incluye seis aventuras diferentes (mediante cartas) de dificultad variable. Eso sí, las partidas no son especialmente largas. Cada una dura una media hora, aproximadamente, pero puedes combinarlas para hacer las tuyas propias o incluso personalizarlas diseñando tus propias variables. Además, como es un juego de LEGO, si tienes tus propios sets aparte, como es mi caso, puedes incluso introducir otros elementos externos (con cuidado, eso sí) para darle otro toque, pero ese ya es otro tema. Volviendo a las aventuras, cada una introduce sus propios desafíos, por lo que se pueden cambiar las condiciones de cada partida según el orden de aparición. Hay motivos para rejugarlo. Y es divertido. Al final, Ninjago: Destiny's Bounty Adventures busca ofrecer una experiencia accesible para compartir en familia que destaca gracias al hecho de que se puede convertir la progresión de los personajes en algo físico de manera natural. Ninjago: Destiny's Bounty Adventures es un juego de mesa cooperativo para entre dos y cuatro jugadores. Cada participante puede escoger a un ninja y el objetivo es defender el Botín del Destino de los villanos de la franquicia. Las partidas se desarrollan mediante seis aventuras diseñadas en cartas. Cada una tiene su propio objetivo final y sus propias condiciones. Antes de empezar, se prepara el tablero usando las normas según el escenario escogido. Luego se colocan los enemigos, distintas fichas y cartas correspondientes. Tras esto, arranca la partida. Se rige por turnos y tienen una estructura muy sencilla. Lo primero es revelar una carta de Evento, la cual puede introducir nuevos enemigos o variaciones del tablero. Luego cada jugador actúa y realiza acciones y, posteriormente, se resuelven los desafíos de cada habitación. Los combates son simples. Cada enemigo tiene una fuerza determinada y para derrotarlo hay que reunir más poder que su fuerza, ya sea en solitario o en grupo. Mientras se progresa, se pueden obtener nuevas piezas de equipo al recorrer el escenario, desde habilidades hasta piezas de equipo. Esto es lo que nos permite modificar al ninja agregando nuevas piezas. Sin embargo, los villanos también avanzan hacia su objetivo. Si consiguen alcanzar las zonas críticas del barco y completar su propio marcador antes de que los ninjas cumplan la misión, el equipo pierde. Por eso, no basta con derrotar enemigos: hay que vigilar las amenazas, aprovechar las habilidades de cada personaje y decidir qué problemas requieren atención inmediata.

articles.title: Why Games Workshop's Falling Share Price Is All of a Sudden in the News
articles.summary: Warhammer 40,000 maker Games Workshop has found itself in the news for its falling share price, which has left some wondering what’s going on behind the scenes.
articles.body:
Warhammer 40,000 maker Games Workshop has found itself in the news for its falling share price, which has left some wondering what’s going on behind the scenes.

Games Workshop is one of the UK's biggest success stories, with its stock rising more than 70% over the past five years. But its share price has fallen 13.76% over the past six months, wiping hundreds of millions of pounds off the value of the company. This comes even as Games Workshop reports record profits. So, what’s going on?

Broadly speaking, there seems to be investor nervousness at Games Workshop’s ability to keep growing in the face of rising manufacturing and logistics costs. Some on the internet will say the recently released 11th edition of flagship tabletop wargame Warhammer 40,000 hasn’t done as well as Games Workshop had hoped, but there is no official data to back this claim up. Indeed, in an update issued mid-September, Games Workshop said that trading to August 30 was “in line with the Board’s expectations for the current financial year.”

Warhammer 40,000 11th Edition Cinematic Trailer: All Shots of the Emperor

However, there is certainly a feeling that Games Workshop may have hit a wall in terms of the popularity of its tabletop games, particularly Warhammer 40,000, which has seen multiple new, pricey miniatures released recently amid claims of over-saturation.

Things ramped up last week with two reports from the financial press about the state of Games Workshop. The first, from the Financial Times , titled ‘Is Warhammer still winning?’ The FT pointed out that while GW’s financials are, broadly speaking, very positive, retail growth per store turned negative for the first time since the pandemic in the second half of its 2026 financial year.

Then there was a report in The Times titled, ‘Games Workshop takes a hammering after mystery report.’ This story claimed a confidential Dragoneye document had wiped £480 million (approx. $635 million) off the company’s value “as the closely guarded contents trigger unease among investors.”

What’s in this Dragoneye document? We don’t know, but The Times said it was about the potential for slowing growth at Games Workshop. It’s interestingly timed, and Dragoneye is a short-focused research firm, so its report should be read with that in mind. Through it all is the obvious point that projecting a slowdown in consumer spending on Games Workshop products shouldn't come as a surprise to anyone. The global economy is struggling, the rising cost of living has caused many to rethink their spending, and AI has everyone spooked about jobs.

So, while some fans are taking to subreddits to express concern about the future of Games Workshop, there is nothing here to indicate the company is in any sort of trouble. Quite the opposite. And let’s not remember what’s in the works for Warhammer. Big hitting video games such as Total War: Warhammer 40,000 and Space Marine 3 are due out in the coming years, and Henry Cavill is soldiering on with his Warhammer 40,000 Cinematic Universe for Amazon. The entertainment push to broaden the appeal of the Warhammer 40,000 IP is surely going to stand Games Workshop in good stead over the years.

And, at the time of this article’s publication, Games Workshop’s share price was up 1.22%. The Emperor, it seems, protects.

articles.title: The Best Books You Can Read In October 2026
articles.summary: From sci-fi to romance and thrillers, here are the best books you'll find on store shelves in October 2026
articles.body:
We don’t know about you, but October is one of our favourite months to get comfortable and settle in with a good book, and there are plenty of them to choose from this month.

From highly anticipated releases from Veronica Roth, V.E. Schwab, and Sarah J. Maas, to new stories by Jason Rekulak and Jane Schoenbrun, there’s something for every type of reader. These are the best new books of October 2026 that are well worth picking up…

Derek Künsken’s The Quantum Evolution series is back, with the fourth book hitting our shelves later this month. And if it happened to pass you by before, or you want to reacquaint yourself with the world before delving into the latest story, there’s still plenty of time to do so.

Book four picks up at the end of the Quantum War, with Belisarius having been sucked into a collapsing wormhole. So, it’s up to Cassandra, Rosalie, Saint Matthew, and their comrade Stills to journey through time itself to find him. But, as you might imagine in a series like this one, things don’t exactly go to plan.

Even with Rosalie’s indicative and potent nightmares seemingly signalling to them from somewhere within the wormhole network, it will take them journeying to its ancient beginnings, and the very dawn of the universe, to hopefully bring him back.

Release date: October 6 (US) and October 8 (UK)

After speaking exclusively to Veronica Roth earlier this summer , we’ve been counting down the days until her latest book – and a return to the Divergent universe – hits our shelves. And the time is finally here.

Instead of being a spin-off, sequel, or prequel, The Sixth Faction asks and answers the question of what could have happened if Beatrice “Tris” made a different choice at her Choosing Ceremony. If you’ve read the previous books or watched the movie adaptations, you’ll know that she ultimately chooses to leave her home and loved ones in Abnegation to join Dauntless.

However, this time tragedy strikes as she makes her decision, changing the course of her future in one fell swoop. And with Roth confirming that this new “book goes into parts of dystopian Chicago that you didn’t see in the original Divergent series,” and “felt like building a new world inside the old one,” we’re so looking forward to being reunited with Tris and the world that we fell in love with all those years ago.

Look What The Cat Dragged In by Jason Rekulak

With Halloween only a few weeks away, if you’re looking for a slightly different take on all things possession, or something just scary enough to make you want to check for any strange goings-on before you settle in to read it, look no further than Jason Rekulak’s Look What The Cat Dragged In.

For those who read his earlier novel, Hidden Pictures , which utilised increasingly unhinged illustrations throughout, his latest book has a new take on this, with the lead character being a talented cartoonist.

The story begins with Penny’s beloved pet cat, Popcorn, going missing. Not only is her cat like a family member to her, but Popcorn also serves as inspiration for her cartoon strips and comic books. Struggling with the grief of losing him and her new reality, when it’s suggested that she pet-sits for another cat, one who immediately warms to her, she hopes that it will help to get her creative spark back.

And well, it does that, just in a way that she would never have anticipated. Let’s just say, when things take a turn, it soon becomes clear that Godfrey is no ordinary cat and more dangerous forces are at work.

The Thrice-Bound Fool by Christopher Buehlman

The second book in Christopher Buehlman’s Blacktongue series, The Thrice-Bound Fool reunites us with professional thief and perennial trickster Kinch Na Shannack. And this time, his life and the lives of all of Manreach depend on one thing: his ability to decipher a truly abominable book. But it’s not just any old book; it’s an ancient tome that is trying to kill him, both when opened and even when it’s closed.

And to make things worse, the all-seeing Taker's Guild doesn't want him to discover the dark magic and hidden secrets held within the book’s pages. So, when Galva, a veteran of the Goblin Wars and Death's sworn handmaiden, agrees to help Kinch and protect him for reasons of her own, could this partnership actually work? You’ll have to pick up a copy to find out.

Off The Reservation by Stephen Graham Jones

Another great horror to pick up in time for spooky season, Stephen Graham Jones – author of My Heart Is A Chainsaw and The Buffalo Hunter Hunter – returns to the world of The Only Good Indians in this follow-up story.

Taking place five years after the horrific massacres on the Blackfeet reservation, survivor Nate Yellow Tail takes this as his opportunity to start life afresh, after a terrible accident that should have taken his life left him on the brink of death.

Lugging his broken body with him, he and three older Blackfeet step aboard a run-down camper van with one aim in mind – to find and repatriate the bones of a fellow Blackfeet member who died at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, where Indigenous children were abused for decades. But, as you might expect, this journey into the past reveals more than they could ever have predicted or expected.

This month brings us the epic conclusion to V.E. Schwab’s Villains trilogy , and we could not be more excited to see how it all wraps up.

Picking up after the incredible showdown with Marcella, Eli, and Serena, the ExtraOrdinary of Merit City have been laying low and doing their best to avoid attracting EON’s attention.

However, with EON now under new leadership, with a horrifying new agenda to boot, they can no longer stay in the shadows. With Victor, Sydney, Mitch, and the rest of them travelling into the enemy’s stronghold at EON headquarters, it’s here that they encounter a number of unforeseen allies, as well as a host of unexpected new abilities, all culminating in the ultimate confrontation. But can they beat the ExtraOrdinary Organization – and the odds – one final time?

Public Access Afterworld by Jane Schoenbrun

For fans of this summer’s cult hit horror movie gem, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma , and 2024’s I Saw the TV Glow , the writer and director of both brings us a fresh new story revolving around a mysterious TV network broadcast, simply known as Public Access Afterworld. And it’s certainly piqued our interest; that’s for sure.

It begins back in 2009, when two suburban teens are sitting together watching TV's transition from analogue to digital. But after the static clears, one of them catches a glimpse of Public Access Afterworld before vanishing into thin air, in turn upending her friend’s life forever.

Fourteen years later, Bethany – a trans content moderator who spends her time sifting through a seemingly endless slew of horrific videos – notices one young streamer call out Public Access Afterworld over and over again. Can Bethany find and rescue them? And what connection does it have to the 2009 disappearance? It’s safe to say that we’ll be picking up a copy.

For those of us who grew up watching comedy classics like Anchorman, Old School, The 40-Year-Old Virgin, and Zoolander, they continue to be some of the most memorable and beloved movies of the time. And in Matt Singer’s Funny Business, we’re given a chance to take a peek behind the scenes at what made those movies so successful and such a big hit with viewers.

Charting the successes of stars who first cut their teeth in improvisational comedy troupes and groups, before making their way onto the likes of SNL, there was a time when you simply couldn’t visit the cinema, or switch on the movie channels, without seeing Ben Stiller, Will Ferrell, Seth Rogen, Vince Vaughn or the Wilson brothers front and centre.

But what happened to that type of comedy? And can they ever make a triumphant return in the age of digital and streaming? Reminiscing and reflecting on the types of comedies that came before, and what could possibly come next, this is a must-read for cinephiles and comedy fans alike.

We always love it when authors get creative with the ways in which they share their stories, and Ali Hazelwood is doing exactly that with the release of Bound and Unbound. Even though both were originally released as audiobooks, this is the first time that they have appeared in print, with Bound on one side and Unbound on the other.

To begin, Bound follows Vero, a down-on-her-luck grad student who is forced to turn to her special talent for forgery to make ends meet. But when her work draws the attention of Dr. Viktor Ashworth, he makes her an offer. However, is it as simple as her helping him forge this mysterious ancient manuscript? Or is there a reason why they seem to be inexplicably drawn together?

Flipping things over to Unbound, this story focuses on the lives of a five-thousand-year-old female revenant, Lilit, and an overworked ER doctor called Roman, who are thrust together. But when someone starts hunting Lilit down and Roman is caught in the crossfire, she must choose between the world that she has sworn to protect and the man she has fallen for. So, whether you’re looking to dip your toe into the world of paranormal fantasy/romantasy or want a change of pace this month, it’s definitely one to try out, especially if you couldn’t get into the audiobook versions.

The Chain House: A Novel by J.H. Markert

With pseudonyms and sometimes even ghostwriters, a lot of the time we’re not always aware of who is behind some of our favourite books and series. And Chain House poses the question: what if a mass murdering cult leader was the author of a bestselling thriller series?

With just days until Sal Batise is set to be executed, he agrees to an interview. However, there is a catch – in order to release his final unpublished manuscript, one which could lead them to finding his victims’ bodies – he wants a stay of execution.

At the same time, a ransom note arrives with a single demand – to save the governor’s recently kidnapped wife – Batise’s execution must go ahead as planned. As the clock ticks down, the young filmmaker, who is conducting the interview, decides to enlist one of the childhood survivors of the cult to help locate the missing manuscript and, in turn, decide the fate of both Batise and the governor’s missing wife.

A Court of Splintered Harmony by Sarah J. Maas

And it wouldn’t be a roundup of the best new books to be released in October 2026 without mentioning the sixth book in Sarah J. Maas’ record-breaking A Court of Thorns and Roses series.

One of the most highly anticipated releases of the entire year, this book centres around Koschei the Deathless and the imminent threat of his return. Obviously, the Night Court won’t be able to stand by and watch while innocents are attacked, but at the same time, rifts and recent betrayals mean that the Night Court isn’t as united and strong as they once were. It will take finding a way to reunite and repair what has broken, if they have any way of surviving and, in turn, defeating Koschei and what is coming their way. With book seven being released in January, it’s definitely a good time to be an ACOTAR fan.

Ellis is a freelance journalist, based in the UK, with a love of all things books. She also routinely chairs bookish events up and down the country, getting the scoop from some of the biggest and bestselling authors to keep you in the know.

articles.title: Why Paying "Market Price" for Rare Pokémon Card Sets Somehow Became The New Normal
articles.summary: Pokémon TCG market prices often exceed MSRP, but they can help collectors avoid scalpers' worst prices, so here's why fans still rely on them.
articles.body:
Even for the biggest and most popular games, getting products at MSRP (Manufacturer’s Suggested Retail Price) should indeed be the norm; nevertheless, for those like the Pokémon TCG , ‘market price’ has become the go-to metric for many collectors for one big reason.

Depending on your perspective as a Pokemon fan, referring to the concept as a gateway to ‘inflated’ or ‘rip-off’ pricing is totally valid.

That said, when actually getting down to the logistics of what it means to get a box of new Pokémon cards at MSRP today, the “market price”, well, market — has been the response to a growing problem with the collectables market as a whole, and is still a legitimate way to enjoy the Pokémon TCG (very much within reason).

Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration Booster Bundle

Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Box

Pokémon TCG: First Partner Illustration Collection—Series 3

Pokémon TCG: Scarlet & Violet—Prismatic Evolutions Super-Premium Collection

Pokémon TCG: Scarlet & Violet - Destined Rivals Elite Trainer Box

Pokémon TCG: Phantasmal Flames Booster Bundle

Buying at MSRP Is Almost Impossible Right Now

To first put it plainly before going into the nitty-gritty, the rise of paying “market price” for Pokemon cards over MSRP ultimately comes down to one classic concept: supply vs. demand.

Over the past couple of years, especially, the demand for the latest boxes of Pokemon cards from new expansions and special collections has gotten so high that supply has consequently not been able to keep up with the demand.

What started all this, of course, was the mainstream discovery of valuable ‘chase cards’ — those regarded with astronomical value due to their rarity, like the famous $1,300+ Umbreon ex from Prismatic Evolutions .

From then on, in a sort of snowball effect, the market became diluted by many buyers buying as much stock as possible, in hopes of pulling the rarest and most expensive cards for profit — nefarious scalpers either flooding retail stores like Costco to physically hoard any stock, or utilising bots to sweep up any stock drops online.

Even if you're regularly online as a full-time remote worker or something similar, any sites selling Pokemon stock either get met with huge crashes, or instanly long queues with everyting sold out at MSRP by the time you can actually get in and shop.

With all of that, you would normally be faced with either needing to practically camp out in front of retail stores before opening hours, or regularly check online stores — such as Best Buy and Target — in hopes of getting lucky to be visiting a site when a stock drop happens. In contrast, the other option is simply giving in to the scalpers and forking over whatever extortionate prices they’re willing to charge.

For Many, "Market Price" is the Tolerable Alternative

Responding to the dire need for some form of regulation in the trading card market, market price estimations are essentially the slightly happier medium option.

Calculated by dedicated online marketplaces like TCGplayer, market price is a way of attempting fair estimation for a product when MSRP isn’t an option — weighing up factors about a card or product like its general rarity, artwork, contents, and any impact it might make on its card game’s meta.

Pokémon TCG: Mega Evolution—Delta Reign Elite Trainer Box

Pokémon TCG: Mega Evolution — Delta Reign Booster Bundle

Pokémon TCG: Mega Evolution—Delta Reign Booster Display Box

Delta Reign Pokemon Center Elite Trainer Box (Exclusive)

Applicable to essentially any other card game like Magic: The Gathering , Yu-Gi-Oh , or the One Piece Card Game , market price has become the new metric for letting Pokemon collectors know whether a higher-than-MSRP price is fair in respect to its demand vs supply, if you’re simply getting ripped off, or if a price is suspiciously so low by comparison, it might be a scammer listing.

For example, there are some eBay sellers charging over $350 for one of the Pokemon TCG’s Ascended Heroes Elite Trainer Boxes; whereas, on TCGplayer, the market price is estimated at a much lower $153.54 — with, at the time of writing, listings there selling for $148 at the lowest .

It’s Still Okay to Be Annoyed About MSRP

While it’s definitely better paying a tamer market price than whatever an unchecked scalper thinks is worthy, it’s also completely fair to remain upset over the current state of the Pokemon TCG, where buying at market price still isn’t feasible.

After all, if the company that makes the actual product declares that said product should only be worth so many dollars or British pounds, it’s right to believe that you should be only paying that price, and not a penny more.

The next go-to thought for anyone just getting into the TCG is that the Pokemon Company should just print enough cards so there’s enough for everyone and eliminate the scalper market altogether.

However, that is actually what the Pokemon Company has been doing. Just last year alone, over 10 billion Pokemon cards were printed ; in context, that’s out of the 85 billion since the card game’s conception — meaning 11% of a 30-year-old card game’s output was carried out in just 12 months.

What’s more, when it comes to the 30th Celebration expansion, vastly improved pull rates for the more in-demand cards have deeply hit scalper operations and have had resellers moan that it isn’t ‘profitable enough’ , since more people getting to pull their chase cards have lowered their market prices as a result.

Despite those major wins for the actual fandoms aside, though, they aren’t enough — at least, not yet. If something is popular enough, tickets, products, goods, etc, will continue to sell despite the controversy around it. In this case, the overall demand for Pokemon TCG cards is still so astronomically high that it still isn’t currently enough to eliminate the need to shop by market price and bring back MSRP as the default.

Those hoarding product just to resell have lost out on some profit incentive, sure, but currently not enough to stop them wanting to spend the time raiding physical and digital shelves entirely. Like the aforementioned snowball effect that kickstarted Pokemon’s lucrative reseller market in the first place, it needs to steadily wind back down in the same way — as more scalpers slowly back out and leave product for the pure fans.

Unfortunately, that will take a long while, and plenty of Pokemon lovers don’t want to take an uncertain amount of time out of the hobby they enjoy. That’s why the ‘market price’ way of buying Pokemon cards is still the go-to metric even now: for those just wanting the best possible price for product that’s readily available — if they don’t want to spend time fighting off scalpers for MSRP — and can make an informed decision as to whether that’s right for them.

For those who can only currently afford to buy Pokemon cards at MSRP, retailer initiatives like Amazon’s invite-only listings are a great way to still score product at their intended price. On the other hand, those required restocks are still being spread across an increasingly keen customer base — making actual invites hard to come by.

Shopping by market price still may not be the perfect resolution for those who only wish to shop by MSRP, but for buyers who wish to buy Pokemon cards at a reasonable rate via the safest method available — it’s in most cases, the best we have until things get better.

Ben Williams – IGN freelance contributor with over 10 years of experience covering gaming, tech, film, TV, and anime. Follow him on Twitter/X @BenLevelTen .

articles.title: Haunted Chocolatier 'More of an Action RPG' Compared to Stardew Valley, ConcernedApe Says
articles.summary: Eric Barone, aka ConcernedApe, has discussed the difference between his all-conquering indie game Stardew Valley and his hotly anticipated follow-up, Haunted Chocolatier.
articles.body:
Eric Barone, aka ConcernedApe, has briefly discussed the difference between his all-conquering indie game Stardew Valley and his hotly anticipated follow-up, Haunted Chocolatier .

Barone announced Haunted Chocolatier back in 2021, but amid ongoing work on his phenomenally successful Stardew Valley, progress on the follow-up has been slow going. Indeed, in June, Barone admitted to feeling somewhat embarrassed to have to keep on saying he was still working away on the game. “Feels kinda dumb posting this same thing over and over, but that’s the reality,” he said at the time.

In a new interview with GQ (thanks, Eurogamer ), Barone touched on what to expect from Haunted Chocolatier when it eventually comes out, and it sounds more different from Stardew Valley than I had expected. It’s set in a more “metaphysical” locale, for a start, and in terms of gameplay it’s more of an action RPG.

“It is still what I call a town game,” Barone said, “But it’s more of an action RPG — the main focus is more about adventuring, finding equipment and getting more powerful. There are monsters, there are boss fights. It's for the people in Stardew Valley that go into the mines. That's what I do, honestly.”

In June, Barone admitted fussing over every last detail in a bid to make Haunted Chocolatier as close to perfect as humanly possible . “I am being very thoughtful about every aspect of the game,” he said at the time. “The things in the game which the player will be interacting with or using very often need to be ‘perfect.’ They need to be seamless, clear, intuitive, satisfying, aesthetic.”

He used the example of iterating on the recipe book for making chocolates, which sounded like a significant challenge.

“To me, it’s not a simple task, as I torture myself over every last detail,” he said. “This is a UI you will be using fairly often, so it has to be perfect. You need to be able to accomplish your goal with the minimal number of clicks. There needs to be just the right amount of data presented to the player: not so much as to be overwhelming, but not so little as to be trivial or mundane. And the way that this data is laid out on the page is crucial… If the data is all clustered together, it will be disgusting to look at. The data needs to be grouped into compelling, intuitive and easy to read/understand groupings. It needs to look appealing and intriguing. And this is just the bare minimum, that players will likely take for granted. If all of that is accomplished then the player is now comfortable while perusing the recipe book. But I want more than just comfort. I want to delight the player. All of this typically requires me to iterate on something several times before I’m satisfied with it.”

Barone also explained why he didn't want to show Haunted Chocolatier off too much at this stage of development. “Partly, it feels like I’m serving a half-baked bread. I would rather serve a fully baked bread,” he said. “Also, I know that many parts of the game will likely evolve and change before release, so if I reveal them early, I risk disappointing players if the final product does not match their expectation. Fortunately, I’m in a position where I don’t need to market the game, so I can take my preferred approach.”

Haunted Chocolatier is so far without a release date, as is Stardew Valley 1.7 update, which Barone isn’t working on directly. Earlier this year, he explained his current way of working in an interview with IGN .

“Well, part of the reason why I've expanded my team a little bit is so that hopefully I can spend more time working on Haunted Chocolatier," he told us in February. "And it's worked out pretty well so far, I would say. On 1.7, the approach we're taking is that I am like, you might say the creative director and I'm involved with like, 'Okay, here's what we're going to do. Here's some of the ideas.' Then I let the team work on that. And then meanwhile, I'm working on Haunted Chocolatier.

"At some point in 1.7's cycle, I will get heavily involved, because I feel like my hand needs to touch every part of the game, every aspect of the update. I need to go over it and adjust it or at least approve everything. So it will require a lot of my time anyway, but I think the balance has been a little bit more shifted, so that I can spend more time focused on Haunted Chocolatier. And I think it's been working out pretty good. That's been a big change from the 1.3 update or 1.1 or something where it's completely me. I had no time to work on a new game. So that has changed.

"It is difficult because it's hard to shift gears, I guess. If I'm thinking about Haunted Chocolatier, it's difficult to be like, 'Okay, I'm going to one day of the week or two days of the week work on Stardew Valley.' That's not how my brain works. I'm all in one thing or the other. So I've been trying to work on that. I feel like it requires a lot of discipline, which I'm always working to improve on."

articles.title: Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration Boosters Are Back in Stock, but Where’s the Best Price Right Now?
articles.summary: Amazon has recently restocked its allocation of Pokémon TCG's 30th Celebration boosters, but prices have skyrocketed to all-new highs.
articles.body:
Amazon has recently restocked its allocation of Pokémon TCG's 30th Celebration Booster Bundles , which are currently available for $99. But is it the best deal going right now?

Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration Booster Bundle

Unfortunately, no, this is still above and beyond MSRP, and considerably more than Amazon was selling the booster bundles for in September ($45).

While TCGplayer is still listing the bundles at over MSRP , it is remarkably better than it was just a few weeks back. There's been a dramatic fall in market value on the 30th Anniversary boosters, dropping 35.43% in just the last month. We were seeing these go for around $120 at the end of September, but you can now pick one up, new and sealed, for about $74 on resale.

It's not great versus the $45 Amazon price we saw last month, but still a lot better than the $99 at Amazon now. I'd expect Amazon to drop their price further in the coming days, in order to shift the new stock allocation, especially since the major retailer does like to try and stick close to market rates when it can.

For $99, you're looking at $16.50 per pack (6 in total). At $74, that brings it down to $12.33 per pack. Still not wonderful, but as I said, not as bad as it could be. If anything, it might be worth holding out in case these drop even further, as I don't expect us trainers will be all too thrilled to be paying $70+ for six boosters.

The 30th anniversary set has been remarkably hard to get hold of ever since preorders went live. The set is now officially available globally, but that doesn't mean the hunt for boosters slows down any time soon.

To nobody’s surprise, the secondary market for the new set is in absolute, unadulterated chaos. Queues have stretched out the IRL doors as long as a Cycling Lane at retailers across the world .

For now, to give you an idea of where the dust is settling, we’ve also recently pulled the median market prices per TCGplayer for the top 10 highest-value cards in the set , so you know what to look out for when ripping packs. See those just below, and good luck!

articles.title: Valor Mortis Is a Novel First-person Soulslike Is Packed With Interesting Ideas, Even If They Don’t Always Work Out Super Smoothly - Review
articles.summary: A novel soulslike packed with interesting ideas, even if they don’t always work out super smoothly.
articles.body:
I’ve gotta hand it to the people at developer One More Level: after well over a decade of countless variations on the soulslike formula, I’ll admit that going first-person with BioShock-like magical abilities shooting out of your hand in an alternate history of the Napoleonic era is… a pretty darn original idea, actually. Valor Mortis is a punishing action game that tries a whole lot of compelling stuff, from combat that mixes sword fighting, spell slinging, and firearms, to the platforming sections that have you wall-running around like you’re in Titanfall, to the bizarre 19th-century setting that kept me guessing. These experiments work out for the most part, and I have many fond memories of dying again and again as I fought my way through this bleak world full of zombified French soldiers. But there are also plenty of moments when this hodgepodge of ideas doesn’t quite come together, not to mention numerous bugs and crashes that turned an otherwise good time into my own personal Waterloo. So while the 20-hour campaign can be a bit uneven, there are still enough interesting things going on in Valor Mortis to make it well worth playing.

If you’ve ever played a BioShock game, you’ll probably feel unexpectedly at home here. Valor Mortis shamelessly cribs the channeling-magic-powers-in-your-corrupted-left-hand concept, and also has the whole alternate history thing going for it as well. But instead of blasting your way through enemies with guns, you’ll mostly be getting up close and personal with a sword, parrying, dodging, and getting killed a whole bunch in the time-honored tradition of the soulslike. It’s an odd combination of things that works out better than I expected, as using your dominant hand for swashbuckling and your off-hand for guns and magical abilities makes for exciting encounters. For example, you might use your mutated arm to light an exploding barrel on fire from afar to take out a group of baddies, block an enemy that’s aggressively rushing you, then back away to finish them off with a pistol. Having so many options for how to deal with deadly enemies helped to hold my interest longer than Valor Mortis otherwise would have, especially given its overall lack of enemy variety.

You play as William, a soldier in Napoleon’s army in an alternate reality where the legendary emperor defeated his enemies at Waterloo, which… well, caused the world to look like a disturbing piece of abstract art, I guess. As an undead warrior with supernatural powers and the ability to come back from death as many times as you need, you fight your way through a series of depressing, war-ravaged areas, meeting a few mostly forgettable characters along the way. Valor Mortis might give off BioShock vibes, but when it comes to story, it falls quite short. It delivers a fairly generic “war is hell” message that’s undermined completely by the silly stuff happening around you, like that time you’re walking in a cave and suddenly find yourself in Egypt fighting off some kind of Spinx thing? I dunno, man. In any case, I’d still say this tries much harder than the average soulslike, but ends up being mostly disappointing.

Valor Mortis’ biggest shortcoming is that, possibly because it tries so many things at once, it can be quite a rocky ride, and that includes its combat. Some of it is minor, weird stuff, like how if you’re fighting big enemies, it feels like you’re hitting them with a pool noodle from several feet away due to some really strange invisible borders. But there are also more concerning issues, like the fact that sometimes enemies will just aim their aggression in a completely different direction, attacking the air or even just standing there while you kill them. And like lots of its peers, Valor Mortis also has that issue where each of the enemies only has a few attacks, so you’ll often just be waiting for them to repeat the same series of strikes for the third time in a row before you can finish them off with an execution. While fighting these gross monsters usually feels just fine, these shortcomings crop up with regularity.

However, a decently sized arsenal of weapons and powers helps to break up that monotony. You have three different melee options, three guns for toting, and three powers to turn your poor hand into a monstrous weapon of war – each with their own upgrade tree to customize how that ability works. For example, you can upgrade your flame ability so that enemies explode if you shoot them with a gun after lighting them on fire, or you can upgrade your saber so that it restores your stamina when you attack after successfully executing a dodge.

Beyond that, you’ve also got a whole skill tree full of perks to choose from and modifiers to equip that help you customize your build a little. Perks offer ways to help William survive a bit better by upping his health or making his parries more effective, but the mods (called Ambers) are more interesting, since they can actually alter the way your character works to suit your playstyle. In my case, I equipped a bunch of mods that made it easier to top off my health, like one that healed me whenever I performed an execution on an enemy whose posture I’d broken – I then equipped another called Perfectionism, which made me do substantially more damage when I was at full health. This allowed me to be a deadly perfectionist, who was rewarded with speedier skirmishes when I successfully managed to avoid taking hits.

Most soulslikes are defined by their memorable boss fights, and this is one area where Valor Mortis feels strangely out of the loop. First off, there are shockingly few of them, to the point where you can make several hours of forward progress without running into one. Secondly, when you eventually do, they are often underwhelming, especially the ones that are just beefier versions of existing enemies or repeated foes you’ve already fought. But even when they are original encounters, they all have the same issue: you’ll mostly just stand around waiting for the boss to pepper you with a ridiculously telegraphed attack so that you can parry it and counter once you’ve broken their posture. I died way more fighting random enemies and falling off of ledges than I did against these wimpy, disappointing bosses. Frankly, it’s probably a good thing there are so few since most aren’t very memorable, and battling through each of the levels against regular minions is much more consistently enjoyable.

One of the best parts about Valor Mortis’ weird-as-heck setting is that it makes for levels that are fairly unique, like the torn-up 19th-century battlefields filled with scattered horse corpses and discarded bayonets, or a harbor of destroyed naval ships that have been raised up into the air unnaturally. You still have plenty of soulslike cliches, like one part where you navigate a flooded village overcome by toxic waters (effectively your poison swamp level if it were created by war crimes), but I was pleasantly surprised by how many areas had personality or some kind of compelling component to pique my interest. For example, one level had me creeping around a ruined town where the only survivors were children who had learned to use their small size to their advantage. Working my way through the destruction while doing my best to gain the favor of these creepy kids was a neat and memorable section that has definitely stuck with me.

Valor Mortis also tries its hand at a bit of platforming, and while I expected it to be pretty top-notch considering the studio’s track record with the Ghostrunner series, most of this sadly feels unpolished. I got caught on ledges, fell through the environment, passed through objects I shouldn’t have, and more, all of which really took the wind out of my sails. To its credit, these parts certainly try some interesting stuff, like one bit where you gain the ability to make platforms appear from afar using one of your nifty hand powers, and grappling through the air and wall running around is quite awesome when it works. But this feels like something that was a little tacked on, given how inconsistently it feels good.

I’ve mentioned a few times that Valor Mortis sometimes feels a bit janky. Some of that is due to specific game design choices and experimentation that doesn’t quite work out, but a much bigger share of that unpolished feel is due to the large amount of technical issues Valor Mortis has. I saw hard crashes, a recurring issue that straight up turned off my PC when I tried to launch from Steam, entire pieces of the environment completely missing, and tons of other wonkiness – the package just has a fairly duct-taped feel to it, which distracted from my journey through this compelling ruined world at times.
